summary: LBURP lets an LDAP client perform a bulk update on an LDAP server. It frames a sequenced set of update operations inside a pair of extended operations, so ordering is preserved even when the updates are sent asynchronously. The document is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like sending a big stack of changes in a labeled bundle so they are applied in the right order.

questions: how does lburp preserve update order
when should i use lburp for directory replication
why is sequence numbering important in bulk updates
subtitle: Protocol for sending bulk updates to an LDAP directory server

tldr.problem: LDAP servers need a way to accept large quantities of updates efficiently while preserving the order of operations, even when updates arrive out of order from the client.
tldr.mechanism: LBURP wraps a sequence of standard LDAP update operations inside a pair of extended operations that mark the start and end of the batch, with sequence numbers on each update so the server can apply them in the correct order regardless of arrival order.
tldr.outcome: Clients can send large batches of updates asynchronously and quickly, and servers can optimize their processing strategy for bulk operations, making directory synchronization and bulk maintenance much faster.

today: RFC 4373 remains the specification for LBURP, an informational protocol. It is suitable for efficiently synchronizing LDAP directory servers in single-master replication scenarios and for bulk administrative updates that must preserve operation order.

sections.title: Problem and Solution
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is the standard way to read and update directory services. An LDAP update operation—adding, modifying, or deleting a directory entry—works fine for small changes, but when a client needs to make hundreds or thousands of updates, the overhead of many individual operations becomes expensive.

LBURP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol Bulk Update/Replication Protocol) solves this by letting a client send a large set of updates as a single batch. The protocol uses standard LDAP update operations but wraps them in a pair of extended operations that tell the server 'here comes a batch' and 'that is the end of the batch.' Each update message carries a sequence number, so the server can process updates in the correct order even if they arrive out of order from the asynchronous network.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of knocking on the door with one change at a time, LBURP lets you show up with a stack of changes. The server knows you are bringing a batch and can apply them all at once, efficiently.

sections.title: How the Protocol Works
sections.content:
LBURP interaction follows a simple three-phase flow. First, the client sends a StartLBURPRequest extended operation, indicating that a bulk update is coming and specifying the update style (the semantics of how to interpret the batch). The server responds with StartLBURPResponse, optionally telling the client the maximum number of update operations to include in each message.

Second, the client sends a stream of LBURPUpdateRequest messages. Each message carries a sequence number (1, 2, 3, ...) and a list of one or more standard LDAP update operations—Add, Modify, Delete, and Modify DN. The operations within each message are applied in list order, and the server applies messages in sequence number order. The server sends an LBURPUpdateResponse after each message, reporting success or listing any operations that failed.

Third, after all updates are sent, the client sends an EndLBURPRequest with a sequence number one greater than the last update message. The server responds with EndLBURPResponse to signal that the batch is complete.

The asynchronous nature of this exchange means the client does not need to wait for a response to one message before sending the next. This maximizes network utilization and client-side throughput.
sections.plainLanguage: Client says 'I am sending a batch.' Server says 'OK, and do not send more than this many changes per message.' Client sends a stream of numbered batches, server answers each one. Client says 'Done,' and server confirms.

sections.title: Structure of Bulk Update Messages
sections.content:
LBURP messages are encoded as LDAP extended operations, using the same Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1) and Basic Encoding Rules (BER) as standard LDAP.

The StartLBURPRequest contains an OID (Object Identifier) that specifies the update semantics. The current RFC defines one style, the Incremental Update style (OID 1.3.6.1.1.17.7), which means apply the updates to the directory as incremental modifications.

Each LBURPUpdateRequest carries a sequence number and an UpdateOperationList—a list of one or more standard LDAP update operations. The operations are encoded exactly as they would be in individual LDAP requests, preserving full compatibility with existing LDAP implementations.

The LBURPUpdateResponse reports results. If all operations in a request succeeded, it simply says success. If any operation failed, the response includes the operation number and the LDAP result (error code and message) for each failure, allowing the client to know exactly which updates succeeded and which did not.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is a numbered list of standard directory commands. If everything works, the server just says OK. If something fails, the server tells you which command failed and why.

sections.title: Update Semantics and Processing
sections.content:
The Incremental Update style, defined in the RFC, is straightforward: the initial state of the directory plus all the updates in the stream define the final desired state. All standard LDAP operations are permitted—Add, Modify, Delete, and Modify DN—with their full semantics. An attempt to add an entry that already exists will fail, just as it would in a normal LDAP Add operation.

The server is free to optimize its processing as long as the final result is as if the updates had been applied in sequence order using standard LDAP operations. For example, a server might buffer updates in memory, disable other LDAP operations during the bulk import, or apply the updates in parallel as long as the order is preserved. This flexibility lets servers make the bulk operation as efficient as possible.

If an update affects multiple Directory System Agents (DSAs, or directory replicas), the server may choose to perform it, return a referral, or chain the request to another server. If a timestamp is not provided by the client, updates are treated as having occurred at the time they were processed.
sections.plainLanguage: Updates are applied in order like normal directory operations. The server can do whatever it wants internally as long as the directory ends up in the right state. If something fails, you find out which operation failed.

sections.title: When LBURP Is Used
sections.content:
LBURP is designed for bulk updates to an LDAP server and for directory replication from a single master to multiple slaves. The protocol is suitable whenever a large set of directory changes need to be made efficiently.

The RFC notes that LBURP does not attempt to solve multiple-master replication, where the same entry might be updated on different replicas at different times. In that scenario, keeping track of modification times and resolving conflicts correctly requires more sophisticated mechanisms beyond the scope of LBURP. Therefore, when LBURP alone is used for replication, proper convergence of data is only assured in a single-master environment.

LBURP is also meant for one-time bulk imports of directory data, directory migrations, and large administrative updates that need to preserve ordering and transaction-like semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: Use LBURP when you have a big stack of directory changes to apply all at once, or when you are syncing a backup copy from a main server. It is not for complex multi-master sync scenarios.

sections.title: Security and Operational Concerns
sections.content:
LBURP adds a potential security risk: because a bulk update stream can contain many operations without the usual per-operation authentication checks, it is crucial that the client connection is properly authenticated and authorized before any LBURP request is accepted. There is no requirement for a pre-existing replication agreement between supplier and consumer, which increases the risk if the server is not careful about who is allowed to initiate a bulk update.

The bulk update stream may contain sensitive data such as passwords. Care should be taken to protect this data in transit. Use of StartTLS, which provides encryption and integrity checking, is recommended.

Because LBURP allows asynchronous updates, a malicious or broken client could send updates faster than the server can process them, potentially overwhelming it. Servers should implement rate limiting or other protections to prevent bulk update operations from interfering with normal LDAP service.

If a server chooses to process a bulk update with special elevated permissions to improve performance, the risks increase further and must be carefully managed.
sections.plainLanguage: Make sure who is sending the batch is allowed to send it. Protect the data in transit, and do not let a bulk update flood the server and break other directory operations.
